items.new: The phantoms, for so they seemed at the time, were flitting on the other side of the deck, and with a noiseless swiftness were casting loose the tackles and bands of the boat that hung there. This boat had always been considered one of the spare boats, though technically it was called the captain's, because it hung from the starboard quarter. The figure that now stood by its bow was tall and dark, with one white tooth evilly protruding from his steel-like lips. A rumpled Chinese jacket of black cotton clothed him funereally, with wide black trousers of the same dark stuff. But strangely crowning all this blackness was a glistening white plaited turban — his own living hair, braided and coiled round and round upon his head. Less dark in appearance, the companions of this figure had that vivid, tiger-yellow complexion peculiar to some of the aboriginal natives of the Manillas — a race notorious for a certain devilish subtlety, and supposed by some honest white sailors to be the paid spies and secret confidential agents, here on the water, of their lord the devil, whose counting-room they suppose to be elsewhere.

items.new: At any time it is a strange sight to the novice to see with what wonderful, unconscious habit of skill the whaleman will keep upright in his boat, even when pitched about by the most riotously perverse and cross-running seas. Stranger still to see him giddily perched on the loggerhead itself in such conditions. But the sight of little Flask mounted on gigantic Daggoo was more curious yet; for, holding himself up with a cool, indifferent, easy, unstudied, barbaric majesty, the noble negro rolled his fine form in harmony with every roll of the sea. On his broad back, flaxen-haired Flask seemed a snowflake. The bearer looked nobler than the rider. True, lively, tumultuous, showy little Flask would now and then stamp with impatience; but he did not add a single heave to the negro's lordly chest by it. So have I seen Passion and Vanity stamping on the living, magnanimous earth, but the earth did not alter her tides and her seasons for that.

items.new: The wind increased to a howl; the waves clashed their shields together; the whole squall roared, forked, and crackled around us like a white fire on the prairie, in which we were burning without being consumed — immortal in these jaws of death! In vain we hailed the other boats; you might as well roar to the live coals down the chimney of a blazing furnace as hail those boats in that storm. Meanwhile the driving spray, flying cloud, and mist grew darker with the shadows of night; no sign of the ship could be seen. The rising sea ruled out any attempt to bail out the boat. The oars were useless for rowing, and now served as life-preservers. So, cutting the lashing of the waterproof match keg, Starbuck, after many failures, managed to light the lamp in the lantern; then, fixing it on a waif pole (the flagged pole used to mark a killed whale), he handed it to Queequeg as the standard-bearer of this forlorn hope. There, then, he sat, holding up that feeble candle in the heart of that almighty forlornness. There, then, he sat, the sign and symbol of a man without faith, hopelessly holding up hope in the midst of despair.

items.new: Ahab knew well that although his friends at home would think little of his getting into a boat during certain comparatively harmless turns of the chase, for the sake of being near the action and giving his orders in person, yet for Captain Ahab to have a boat actually assigned to him as a regular headsman in the hunt — above all, for Captain Ahab to be supplied with five extra men as that boat's crew — he knew well that such generous notions never entered the heads of the owners of the Pequod. So he had not asked them for a boat's crew, nor had he in any way hinted at his wishes on that score. Nevertheless, he had taken private measures of his own in the whole matter. Until Cabaco's discovery was made public, the sailors had little foreseen it. To be sure, once they had been a little while out of port and all hands had finished the customary business of fitting out the whaleboats for service, Ahab was, some time after this, now and then found busying himself with making thole-pins (the pegs that hold the oars in place) with his own hands for what was thought to be one of the spare boats, and even carefully cutting the small wooden skewers that are pinned over the groove in the bow when the line is running out; when all this was noticed in him, and particularly his concern to have an extra layer of sheathing in the bottom of the boat, as if to make it better withstand the pointed pressure of his ivory limb; and also the anxiety he showed in shaping exactly the thigh-board, or clumsy cleat, as it is sometimes called — the horizontal piece in the boat's bow for bracing the knee against when darting or stabbing at the whale; when it was noticed how often he stood up in that boat with his single knee fixed in the semicircular hollow in the cleat, and with the carpenter's chisel gouged out a little here and straightened it a little there — all these things, I say, had stirred much interest and curiosity at the time. But almost everybody supposed that this particular care in preparation on Ahab's part could only be with a view to the final chase of Moby Dick, for he had already revealed his intention to hunt that mortal monster in person. But such a supposition by no means involved the faintest suspicion that any boat's crew would be assigned to that boat.

items.new: But be all this as it may, it is certain that while the subordinate phantoms soon found their place among the crew — though still, as it were, somehow distinct from them — that hair-turbaned Fedallah remained a muffled mystery to the last. Where he came from, in a well-mannered world like this; by what unaccountable sort of tie he soon showed himself to be linked with Ahab's peculiar fortunes — indeed, so far as to have some sort of half-hinted influence; Heaven knows, it might even have been authority over him — all this nobody knew. But no one can keep up an air of indifference about Fedallah. He was such a creature as civilized, domestic people in the temperate zone see only in their dreams, and even then only dimly; but the like of him now and then glide among the unchanging Asiatic communities, especially the Oriental islands to the east of the continent — those isolated, immemorial, unalterable countries which even in these modern days still keep much of the ghostly aboriginal quality of earth's first generations, when the memory of the first man was a distinct recollection, and all men, his descendants, not knowing where he came from, eyed each other as real phantoms, and asked the sun and the moon why they were created and to what end; when, though according to Genesis the angels indeed consorted with the daughters of men, the devils also, add the uncanonical rabbis, indulged in earthly love affairs.

items.new: The ostensible reason why Ahab did not go on board the whaler we had spoken — that is, hailed at sea — was this: the wind and sea signaled storms. But even had this not been the case, he would not, perhaps, have boarded her after all — judging by his later conduct on similar occasions — if it had turned out that by hailing he had got a negative answer to the question he put. For, as it eventually turned out, he did not care to keep company, even for five minutes, with any stranger captain unless that captain could contribute some of the information he so absorbingly sought. But all this might not be properly appreciated unless something were said here about the peculiar customs of whaling vessels when they meet each other in foreign seas, and especially on a common cruising-ground.

items.new: So, then, we see that of all ships sailing the sea separately, the whalers have the most reason to be sociable — and they are. Some merchant ships, on the other hand, crossing each other's wake in the mid-Atlantic, will often pass on without so much as a single word of recognition, cutting each other dead on the high seas like a pair of dandies on Broadway, and all the while indulging, perhaps, in fussy criticism of each other's rig. As for men-of-war, when they happen to meet at sea, they first go through such a string of silly bowings and scrapings, such a dipping of flags, that there does not seem to be much downright hearty goodwill and brotherly love about it at all. As for slave-ships meeting — why, they are in such a tremendous hurry that they run away from each other as soon as possible. And as for pirates, when they happen to cross each other's cross-bones, the first hail is "How many skulls?" — the same way whalers hail "How many barrels?" And once that question is answered, pirates steer apart at once, for they are infernal villains on both sides and don't like to see too much of each other's villainous likenesses.
